digest.top_line: Single-fraction SBRT (12 or 16 Gy) vs 30 Gy/10fx for nonspine bone mets: ITT 3-mo pain response 38% vs 21% (P=.05), 24-mo local failure 0% vs 9.7%.
digest.tldr: Ablative RT carried the day: a randomized phase 2 favors single-fraction SBRT over 30 Gy/10fx for nonspine bone mets on pain and local control, while a 9-expert survey shows wide practice spread with 35 Gy/5 most chosen. Ultra-central lung SBRT meta-analysis pools 2-yr LC 89% at G5 toxicity 4%; 4 Gy LD-IFRT gives ORR 92% in recurrent indolent lymphoma.

sites.intro: Nonspine bone SBRT: randomized single-fraction vs 30 Gy/10fx data next to an expert survey of how dose is actually chosen.

studies.name: Nonspine Bone Metastases SBRT International Practice Patterns
studies.tldr: 35 Gy/5 most chosen (29 of 99 responses) and 40 Gy/5 most accepted across 11 NSBM cases; all 9 experts prescribed BED ≤100 Gy10.

details.text: 🔍 Survey of 9 international radiation oncologists, 11 nonsurgical NSBM cases, 100% completion

details: 🔍 Cases covered long (femur, humerus), pelvic and thoracic bones; RCC, breast, NSCLC, prostate histologies
🔍 GTV pre-contoured and sent with planning CT + MRI; descriptive analysis only

📊 35 Gy/5 chosen in 29 of 99 responses (29%); 5 experts used it in ≥1 case
📊 40 Gy/5 judged acceptable unanimously (n=9) or near-unanimously (n=8) wherever listed
📊 SIB used by 3 experts; 30 Gy/3 + 15-24 Gy/3 most common (12 of 24, 50%)
🔍 MRI fusion routine for 5 experts (56%); 2 CT-only; 2 fuse MRI selectively
📊 Schedules a majority of experts did NOT recommend, by site
📊 Factors changing dose selection (n experts)

details: 📊 Unanimous: no dose change for mild cortical erosion or non-weight-bearing bone with moderate-severe erosion

details.text: 🔗 vs Erler et al: 30-35 Gy/5 gave LC 95% at 6 mo, 87% at 24 mo (106 NSBM)
🔗 Same series: fracture 8.5%, median time to fracture 2.5 mo after 30-35 Gy/5

details: ⚠️ No formal consensus process; expert opinion only, no outcomes measured

details.text: ⚠️ BED computed at α/β 10, which overstates equivalence for breast and prostate histologies

verdict.rationale: Expert practice-pattern survey (9 radiation oncologists, 11 cases); no formal consensus process and no outcomes measured. Acceptability figures are opinion, not efficacy.
verdict.audience: Nonsurgical nonspine bone mets (long, pelvic, thoracic bones) planned for SBRT

studies.significance: The dose ceiling is the RT read: every expert stayed at BED ≤100 Gy10, below the >100 Gy10 threshold used for lung and liver SBRT, and site mattered more than histology. Single-fraction 20 Gy/1 drew majority rejection in humerus, acetabulum and femur, and 50 Gy/5 in humerus and acetabulum, which frames fractionation choice for weight-bearing long bones and joints.
studies.monday_clinic: In a nonsurgical nonspine bone met planned for SBRT, especially weight-bearing bone with moderate-severe cortical erosion or prior RT to the site, this supports a 5-fraction schedule over single-fraction dosing; it does not establish local control or fracture rates for any schedule.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Two-round survey of **9 international radiation oncologists** (Canada, US, Australia, Switzerland, Netherlands, Korea) over **11 NSBM cases**. Round 2 rated each proposed schedule acceptable / not recommended / no opinion and picked 2 preferred; **majority defined as ≥5 of 9**. No formal consensus-building process.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Cases chosen to span long bones (femur, humerus), pelvic bones (ilium, ischium, acetabulum, pubic symphysis) and thoracic bones (rib, sternum, scapula, clavicle); RCC, breast, NSCLC and prostate primaries. All cases specified **nonsurgical**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: 6 experts prescribed **1 dose volume**, 3 used an **SIB** to GTV/CTV1 vs CTV/CTV2 (e.g. 30 Gy/3 to GTV or CTV1, 15-24 Gy/3 to CTV or CTV2). **5 experts (56%)** routinely fused MRI with planning CT.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **35 Gy/5** was the most chosen schedule and **40 Gy/5** the most widely accepted; 35 Gy/5 and 40 Gy/5 drew the most preferred votes in each case. Scapula was the only case where every schedule had majority acceptance.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective NSBM series cited by the authors report **LC 95% and 87% at 6 and 24 mo** after 30-35 Gy/5 (Erler et al, 106 lesions) and **1-yr LC 92%** across 15 Gy/1 to 50 Gy/5 (85 lesions). A phase II trial cited showed better pain response with single-fraction SBRT vs cRT, though its target delineation and dose were institutional.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents nonsurgical nonspine bone metastases treated with SBRT at expert centres. Does not represent spine metastases or lesions where an OAR constraint forces de-escalation.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: BED computed at **α/β 10**, which the authors acknowledge misfits breast and prostate. International health-system and resource differences confound the spread of practice, and several authors report industry ties (Elekta, Varian, Accuray).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Agreement clusters around **5-fraction schedules**, a BED ceiling of 100 Gy10, and de-escalation for prior RT and weight-bearing bone with cortical erosion. The optimal dose balancing LC against fracture is **unknown**; the authors call for phase I dose-finding and comparative trials.

studies.interpretation:
What this paper offers is a map of where expert judgment converges and where it splits, and the convergences are more useful than the headline about heterogeneity. Nine experienced practitioners, working from identical pre-contoured cases, independently landed below a BED of 100 Gy10 for every schedule they chose. That is a lower ceiling than the >100 Gy10 threshold the authors cite for lung and liver SBRT, and it reflects a shared instinct that bone, particularly bone that carries load or sits beside a joint, tolerates ablative dose poorly. The reader should treat that instinct as a prior, not a finding. Nothing in this survey measured fracture, local control, or pain; the ceiling is caution made visible.

The site-level pattern is the more transferable signal. Single-fraction 20 Gy/1 was rejected by a majority in the humerus, acetabulum and femur cases, and 50 Gy/5 in the humerus and acetabulum, while the scapula case accepted every option. Read together, the experts are sorting by mechanical risk rather than by histology: the dose-escalation factors they named (radioresistant histology, bulk, extraosseous extension) drew only a minority, whereas prior RT and weight-bearing bone with cortical erosion drove de-escalation in most. For a radiation oncologist planning a proximal femur or acetabular lesion, that is the practical takeaway: fractionating is the expert default, and single high doses in those locations sit outside the comfort zone of this panel.

Against the existing evidence, the survey sits on thin ground by the authors' own account. The local-control figures they cite come from retrospective series, one using 30-35 Gy/5, so a preference for 35 Gy/5 partly reproduces the schedule that generated the data. The cited phase II trial favouring single-fraction SBRT over conventional RT for pain is in some tension with this panel's reluctance about single fractions in long bones, and the gap is unexplained: either the trial population was weighted toward lower-risk sites, or expert caution about fracture is outrunning the evidence. The survey cannot say which.

Methodologically, three choices should temper confidence. The panel is small and selected for expertise, so it reports practice at centres that already do this often, not the field. No consensus process was run, so the acceptability counts reflect independent ratings that were never reconciled through discussion. And the BED arithmetic assumes an α/β of 10 across a case set that includes breast and prostate primaries, which flattens real biological differences between schedules for those histologies; two schedules that look equivalent at α/β 10 may not be for a breast metastasis.

What would make this wrong is prospective data showing that single-fraction or higher-BED regimens in weight-bearing bone carry no excess fracture risk while improving control, which would reframe the panel's caution as conservatism without cost. Until dose-finding and comparative trials report, the paper supports using a 5-fraction schedule in the 35-40 Gy range as a defensible middle ground, and documenting the mechanical rationale when departing from it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Every expert held BED ≤100 Gy10, under the lung and liver threshold, and rejected 20 Gy/1 by majority in humerus, acetabulum and femur. That points fractionation choice for weight-bearing long bones and periarticular lesions toward 5-fraction schedules, with de-escalation for prior RT or moderate-severe cortical erosion.

studies.name: Single-Fraction SBRT vs Multifraction RT for Nonspine Bone Metastases
studies.tldr: Single-fraction SBRT (12 or 16 Gy) vs 30 Gy/10fx: ITT 3-mo pain response 38% vs 21% (P=.05); local failure 0% vs 9.7% at 24 mo.
details: 🔍 Single-institution (MD Anderson) randomized phase 2 noninferiority trial, nonblinded, N=160 (81 SBRT, 79 MFRT)
🔍 SBRT 12 Gy (>4 cm) or 16 Gy (≤4 cm) x1 vs 30 Gy/10fx
🔍 PTV = GTV + 5mm, no CTV; prophylactic 7-day low-dose dexamethasone recommended for SBRT
📐 1° EP pain response (CR+PR) per international consensus criteria; NI margin 10%, 1-sided α 0.20, 90% power

details.text: 📊 Pain response (CR+PR) by population and timepoint
📊 Pain response by dose, SBRT ITT subset (dose assigned by lesion size, not randomized)
📊 Local control, reirradiation and OS
📐 ITT hazard ratios at 3 mo, SBRT vs MFRT
subdetails: Composite pain failure (PP + IR): HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.16-3.27)

details.text: 📊 No toxicity differences between arms

details: ⚠️ Superiority signal comes from the per-protocol analysis; ITT 1-mo difference P=.18
⚠️ Comparator was 30 Gy/10fx, not 8 Gy x1
⚠️ 5 SBRT pts not treated due to insurance denial; no equivalent loss in the control arm
⚠️ Size cut-point for 12 vs 16 Gy stated inconsistently (≥4 cm vs >4 cm for 12 Gy)

verdict.rationale: Single-institution randomized phase 2 at 1-sided α 0.20; superiority rests on shrinking per-protocol subsets. Authors themselves call for phase 3 validation.
verdict.audience: Painful, predominantly nonspine bone mets, life expectancy >3 mo

studies.significance: The dose split matters most: at 3 mo, 16 Gy (lesions ≤4 cm) gave 62% CR+PR vs 30% for 12 Gy and 21% for 30 Gy/10fx, and 42.9% vs 13.3% vs 15.2% at 9 mo. Lesion size set the dose, so 12 Gy for larger lesions adds little over the long course, and the trial never tested 8 Gy x1.
studies.monday_clinic: In good-PS pts with limited, painful nonspine bone mets and longer expected survival, this supports single-fraction SBRT as an alternative to 30 Gy/10fx; it does not inform pts with untreated cord compression, pathologic fracture, or prior RT to the site.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 2, nonblinded, randomized noninferiority** trial at one institution (MD Anderson), 1:1, N=160, enrolled 2014-2018. Stratified by tumor size, site and number of sites irradiated.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Painful bone mets (pain score ≥2), life expectancy >3 mo**, age ≥18, up to 3 fields allowed. Excluded prior RT to the site, untreated cord compression, pathologic fracture, and recent radioisotope therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 12 Gy (>4 cm) or 16 Gy (≤4 cm) x1 vs 30 Gy/10fx.** PTV = GTV + 5mm with no CTV in either arm; stereotactic immobilization for SBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** pain response (CR+PR) by international consensus criteria, combining pain score and MED. **Secondary:** MDASI QoL, CTCAE toxicity, local control, OS.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: ITT noninferiority claimed for pain and local control; the clearer superiority separations are per-protocol (see tables). **No OS difference** (median 6.7 mo both arms).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No differences in toxicity.** G3 fatigue 9.9% SBRT vs 5.1% MFRT (P=.37); fracture 1.2% vs 0%; dermatitis 1.2% vs 2.5%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Older randomized comparisons such as RTOG 9714 and the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study found single and multifraction courses equivalent for pain, with more retreatment after the low-dose single fraction. This trial escalated the single fraction but tested it against the long course, **not against the low-dose single fraction** most practices already use.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents good-PS pts with painful, predominantly nonspine bone mets and life expectancy >3 mo. Does not represent spine mets with cord compression, pathologic fracture, or previously irradiated sites.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Patient-reported primary in an **unblinded** trial with differential attrition. The 16 vs 12 Gy split is confounded by lesion size, and local PFS beyond 1y rests on single-digit to high-teen numbers at risk.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The gain may sit mainly in small lesions treated to **16 Gy**, with 12 Gy offering little over 30 Gy/10fx. Whether ablative single-fraction dose beats 8 Gy x1 for durable palliation is **not settled** here.

studies.interpretation:
This trial answers a narrower question than its title suggests. The reference arm was 30 Gy in 10 fractions, a regimen many palliative services had already left behind for a single 8 Gy fraction, on the strength of older randomized comparisons that the authors summarize as showing equal pain control with more retreatment after the short course. So escalated single-fraction SBRT against 8 Gy, the comparison that matters for current practice, was not tested. What the trial does show is that an ablative single fraction is at least not worse than the long course for pain, and may be better for local control. That holds in a population where many pts did not live long enough for durability to matter: median OS was 6.7 months in both arms.

The statistics should temper confidence. Noninferiority was declared at a 1-sided alpha of 0.20, a permissive phase 2 threshold, and the extracted text never reports the confidence limit of the response difference against the 10% margin. The ITT difference had P=.18 at 1 month and P=.05 at 3 months. The clearer separations at 2 weeks, 3 months and 9 months come from the per-protocol population. That population shrank to 43 vs 35 evaluable pts at 3 months and 22 vs 26 at 9 months after deaths, dropout and ineligibility. A nonblinded trial with a patient-reported endpoint and uneven attrition is exactly where a per-protocol advantage tends to inflate. Five SBRT pts were never treated because insurance refused coverage, a selection step the control arm did not have.

The dose subset is the most interesting signal and the hardest to defend. At 3 months, 16 Gy gave 62% response, against 30% for 12 Gy and 21% for the long course. But lesion size decided the dose, so the 16 Gy pts had smaller lesions, and small lesions may respond better at any dose. The paper also gives the size cut-point inconsistently between its Key Points and Methods. Read honestly, any SBRT advantage may sit with small lesions treated to 16 Gy. The 12 Gy experience in larger lesions offers little over 30 Gy/10fx.

Local control favored SBRT, with no local failures against 9.7% cumulative incidence at 24 months. But the HR for local failure was 0.18 with a CI of 0.02-1.47, and numbers at risk after the first year were small. Reirradiation did not differ statistically (P=.10). The QoL-adjusted survival advantage uses the Q-TWiST method on top of an OS difference of zero, and a nonblinded symptom inventory drives it.

The decision this informs is selection. A pt with good performance status, limited bone disease, and a reasonable expectation of outliving this trial's median is where a durability or local-control advantage could pay off, and those are the pts a confirmatory phase 3 should enroll. For the median pt here, the real gain is the convenience of one fraction, which 8 Gy already offers. Anyone who would change practice on this trial should change it toward 16 Gy for small lesions in pts expected to live longer, and should do so knowing that this rests on a nonrandomized subset.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The dose split matters most: 16 Gy (≤4 cm) gave 62% CR+PR at 3 mo vs 30% for 12 Gy and 21% for 30 Gy/10fx, and 42.9% vs 13.3% vs 15.2% at 9 mo. Lesion size set the dose, and the trial never compared against 8 Gy x1.

open_questions: Does 16 Gy SBRT beat 8 Gy single fraction for nonspine bone mets?
Does the 16 vs 12 Gy dose response hold under randomization?
Which pts live long enough to benefit from SBRT durability?

studies.name: Low-Dose Involved Field RT in Indolent Lymphomas
studies.tldr: 4 Gy involved-field RT: ORR 92%, CR 61%, median TP 14 mo and TLP 25 mo in symptomatic recurrent indolent lymphoma, toxicity virtually absent.
details: 🔍 Phase II, 109 assessable of 111 treated, 304 symptomatic sites, Nov 1997 to Mar 2002
🔍 Symptomatic recurrent B-cell indolent lymphoma: FL 98 (G1 43, G2 55), MALT 9, lymphoplasmacytoid 2
🔍 Median 2 prior regimens; 50% refractory to last regimen; bulky ≥5cm in 52%
🔍 RT: 4 Gy as 2×2 Gy 48h apart (n=80) or 1×4 Gy (n=29); whole nodal area or node + 1.5cm margin

details.text: 📊 Time to progression by response to first LD-IF-RT
📊 First course vs LD-IF-RT re-treatment (selected responders)

details: 📊 Toxicity virtually absent: 1 transient alopecia, 1 transient hyperpigmentation, no tumor lysis
📐 RR vs prior regimens: better than 2nd (P=.04) and last (P=.03); no difference vs 1st (P=.08)
⚠️ Median f/u for pts still in remission only 7 mo
🔗 vs Girinsky (Paris) series: similar RR and CR, but 2y local PFS in PR pts 46% vs 10% here

verdict.rationale: Single-arm phase II with no randomised comparator; median follow-up in remission only 7 mo, and prior-regimen comparisons are within-patient and confounded by line.
verdict.audience: Symptomatic recurrent indolent B-cell lymphoma (mostly FL G1-2), median 2 prior lines

studies.significance: Response depth sets how long 4 Gy controls the site: PR pts relapsed in-field first (median TLP 10 mo) while CR pts held local control for a median 42 mo. Re-treatment of selected responders still gave RR 98%, so one low-dose course does not rule out another at relapse.
studies.monday_clinic: In symptomatic recurrent FL G1-2 or MALT lymphoma, including chemorefractory disease, this supports 4 Gy as a repeatable local palliative option; it does not extend to stage I-II, transformed, or curative-intent disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase II** single-arm series, 111 treated and **109 assessable**, 304 irradiated sites. **Primary:** in-field lymphoma control, response graded on local disease only.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Symptomatic recurrent B-cell indolent lymphoma**; transformed disease and concurrent steroids or chemo excluded. FL 98 of 109, median age 62, median 2 prior regimens, bulky ≥5cm in 52%. Stage I and II pts not enrolled.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **4 Gy** as 2×2 Gy 48h apart (n=80) or 1×4 Gy (n=29). Target was the whole nodal area or the node with a **1.5cm margin**, at physician discretion; involved sites only, no elective coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: ORR 92%, CR 61%. Median TP 14 mo, median TLP 25 mo. Fraction schedule, FL grade, prior regimens and largest diameter were **not related to response rate**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity **virtually absent**: one transient alopecia, one transient hyperpigmentation. No gout or tumor lysis syndrome with allopurinol in bulky disease.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Consistent with the Girinsky Paris series on RR, CR and inferior control at bulky sites, but 2y local PFS in PR pts was 46% there vs 10% here. The later randomised FoRT trial tested this low-dose schedule against conventional-dose RT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents symptomatic recurrent FL G1-2 or MALT lymphoma after systemic therapy, including chemorefractory disease. Does not represent stage I-II, transformed, or curative-intent disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Any chemo or steroid, even for a nonmalignant indication, counted as local failure, which biases TLP downward. Target volume varied by physician, and CR-rate signals for ≤2 sites (P=.01) and ≤5cm nodes (P=.006) sit among many comparisons.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for 4 Gy here is low toxicity, rapid response and repeatability rather than durable control. It positions low-dose RT as a palliative tool between watchful waiting and another systemic line, not as a substitute for conventional dose where long local control matters.

studies.interpretation:
This series is best read as the paper that turned 2×2 Gy from an anecdote into a usable palliative tool for recurrent indolent lymphoma. Its contribution is not the headline response rate, which earlier smaller series had already suggested, but the demonstration that the response holds in a heavily pretreated, half chemorefractory population and that a second low-dose course works in selected responders. For a radiation oncologist the practical message is that a symptomatic node in a pt several lines deep can be treated in one or two visits with almost no toxicity cost.

The more instructive finding is how strongly durability tracks response depth. Pts reaching CR held in-field control for a median 42 mo, while PR pts failed in-field first with a median TLP of 10 mo, essentially the same as their overall time to progression. That pattern argues that 4 Gy either clears a site or buys a short interval, and that a PR after low-dose RT behaves more like undertreatment than partial benefit. The divergence from the Girinsky Paris series on PR durability is worth taking seriously; the authors attribute it to Paris enrolling early-stage pts, which would also explain why that series found age and prior lines predictive and this one did not.

Several methodological choices should temper confidence in the time-to-event numbers in both directions. The local-failure definition counted any chemotherapy or corticosteroid exposure, even for COPD, as an event, which makes TLP conservative. Against that, median follow-up for pts still in remission was only 7 mo, so the tail of the local-control curve rests on few pts. The comparison against each pt's prior regimens is creative but confounded: later lines are expected to do worse, so outperforming the second and last regimen says more about the trajectory of relapsed FL than about the relative efficacy of RT. Target volume was left to physician discretion, so the series does not tell you whether a whole nodal area or node plus 1.5cm is the better field.

What the series does not settle is the dose question itself. It establishes that 4 Gy is active, not that it is equivalent to conventional dose; that comparison was later addressed in the randomised FoRT trial, and the short local control in PR pts here is the signal that made that question necessary. It also says nothing about early-stage disease, where curative intent changes the calculus, or about how low-dose RT sequences with rituximab-based therapy, which postdates most of this cohort's prior lines.

For a skeptic, the single-arm design and the absence of any toxicity grading scale are the main weaknesses, along with ten transformations whose median TP was only 3 mo, a reminder that a fast in-field response does not exclude biology that will outrun local therapy. The result would be wrong in practice if the 7 mo follow-up concealed late in-field failures among CR pts, which the immature tail cannot exclude.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Response depth predicts local durability: CR sites held in-field control for a median 42 mo, PR sites failed in-field at a median 10 mo. Fraction schedule (2×2 vs 1×4 Gy) was not related to response, and re-treatment of responders gave RR 98%.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Half the cohort was refractory to its last regimen, yet chemorefractory and chemosensitive pts had similar RR, CR rate and median TP. For a symptomatic site late in the disease course, 4 Gy is a near-toxicity-free option before committing to another systemic line.

studies.name: SBRT for Ultra-Central Lung Tumors: Meta-Analysis and ISRS Guidelines
studies.tldr: Pooled 1-yr LC 92% and 2-yr LC 89%, with G5 toxicity 4%, across 1183 pts with ultra-central lung tumors; ISRS sets PBT Dmax and fractionation limits.

details.text: 🔍 SR/MA of 27 studies (2010-2022), 1183 pts, random-effects model

details: 🔍 All retrospective except HILUS (prospective phase 2 observational); none randomized
🔍 Ultra-central definition varied: PTV-PBT overlap in all studies, GTV overlap in only 16 (59%)

details.text: 📊 Pooled estimates
📊 NSCLC-only subset: 1- and 2-yr LC both 95%
📐 Higher BED linked to 1-yr LC (HR 2.14, p=0.03); no 2-yr association (p=0.66)
📊 Hemoptysis caused most G5 events (42 events, 58%); G5 range across studies 0-22%
🔍 ISRS recommendations by category

Dmax <133-150 Gy BED3 (EQD2 α/β=3 <80-90 Gy); lower if risk factors or near trachea/main bronchi
Discontinue when pausing is low risk; else de-escalate PBT Dmax or use non-SBRT schedule
Avoid concomitant use; ≥2-3 days for targeted, 3-4 wk for VEGF inhibitors, ≥2 days for IO

Lung V20 <10% strict cutoff; treat on trial

details.text: 🔗 HILUS G5 hemoptysis 4% if >1 cm from main bronchi/trachea vs 18% if ≤1 cm

details: ⚠️ PBT Dmax showed no association with toxicity on meta-regression; too few studies reported dosimetry

details.text: ⚠️ 60% of studies had median f/u <2 yr; late hemoptysis likely under-captured

details: ⚠️ Publication bias detected across all LC and toxicity endpoints

verdict.rationale: ISRS recommendations rest on 27 studies, only HILUS prospective and none randomized, with high heterogeneity and publication bias. Constraints are expert synthesis, not tested thresholds.
verdict.audience: Ultra-central lung tumors (PTV abutting PBT), primary NSCLC or metastases

studies.significance: The usable output is the PBT constraint: Dmax <133-150 Gy BED3 (EQD2 80-90 Gy), prescribed to an 80-85% IDL, dropping to 60 Gy/15 with Dmax <100 Gy BED3 for endobronchial disease. Pooled meta-regression could not test PBT Dmax, so the threshold rests on HILUS, Tekatli, Mihai and Wang dosimetry.
studies.monday_clinic: For an ultra-central NSCLC or lung metastasis with PTV overlapping the PBT, this supports 60 Gy/8 or 60 Gy/15 with hotspot control over a HILUS-style 67% IDL plan; it does not make SBRT routine for endobronchial, ILD, or recently VEGF-exposed pts.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA/MOOSE) of **27 studies, 1183 pts**, published 2010-2022; random-effects pooling with meta-regression on BED, PTV volume and PBT Dmax. **All retrospective except HILUS**; none randomized. Median follow-up ranged 7.6-44.5 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Ultra-central lung tumors treated with SBRT (≥5 Gy/fx, photons), ≥5 eligible lesions per study. Excluded reirradiation and hilar/mediastinal nodal targets. Only 9 studies (33%) were **entirely primary NSCLC**; the rest mixed in metastases.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Doses 30-70 Gy in 3-10 fx; most common **50 Gy/5 (18%)**, **60 Gy/8 (17%)** and **60 Gy/12 (10%)**, BED10 range 52.5-180. Motion management in 96%, mostly 4DCT. OAR dosimetry reporting was variable.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **Any G5 4%** (95% CI 2-6), range 0-22% across studies, with 7 studies reporting ≥10%. Hemoptysis caused 58% of G5 events; G5 pneumonitis pooled at 0%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Pooled 2-yr LC of 89% sits with **RTOG 0813** (89.4% in central/ultra-central tumors) and the SBRT arm of **TROG 09.02** (89%, noncentral). Toxicity is lower than an earlier 250-pt review (treatment-related mortality 5%) and far below **HILUS** (G5 15%), which the authors attribute to a 67% IDL and margins up to 15 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ultra-central primary NSCLC and lung metastases treated with SBRT using motion management and conservative fractionation. Does not represent endobronchial tumors, ILD, or pts on VEGF inhibitors or anticoagulation, where fatal events clustered.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **PBT Dmax showed no association with toxicity** on meta-regression because few studies reported dosimetry, so the pooled analysis cannot validate the constraint it recommends. Most studies had median follow-up <2 yr, which undercounts late hemoptysis; PBT substructure sensitivity could not be resolved beyond HILUS.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The pooled data say ultra-central SBRT can control tumors at rates matching central and peripheral series; the real question is where fatal risk concentrates. The guideline's answer is anatomy (trachea/main bronchi), hotspot placement and concomitant risk factors, all drawn from individual series rather than pooled modelling. **SUNSET** and **LUNGTECH** are the pending prospective tests.

studies.interpretation:
The headline numbers are reassuring, but the useful content of this paper is in what the pooled estimate cannot show. A 4% pooled grade 5 rate sits awkwardly beside HILUS at 15%, and the range across included series runs from 0 to 22%. That spread is not noise around a single truth. It suggests fatal toxicity concentrates in a definable subset (tumors closest to the trachea and main bronchi, endobronchial disease, pts on anticoagulation or VEGF inhibitors, ILD) and is diluted when those cases are pooled with tumors that merely graze the PBT. The pooled 1% grade 5 hemoptysis figure describes the average plan, not the plan that kills.

The guideline handles this honestly in one respect and optimistically in another. Honestly, because the authors say plainly that meta-regression found no relationship between PBT Dmax and bronchial toxicity, and attribute that to sparse dosimetry reporting rather than to an absent effect. The recommended ceiling of 133-150 Gy BED3 is therefore assembled from individual cohorts (HILUS, Tekatli, Mihai, Wang) whose fatal cases sat above it, not derived from a pooled dose-response curve. That is reasonable expert synthesis, but a reader should treat it as a constraint informed by cases rather than a validated threshold. Optimistically, because the explanation offered for HILUS, a 67% isodose prescription pushing central PTV dose toward 150% plus margins up to 15 mm, is plausible and fits the dosimetry, yet it remains a post hoc reading of one trial. The recommendation to prescribe to an 80-85% isodose line follows directly from that interpretation and has not been tested prospectively.

The efficacy side carries less risk of misreading. A 2-yr LC of 89% sits beside RTOG 0813 and TROG 09.02, and the NSCLC-only subset at 95% suggests mixed histology is not inflating the result. The BED dose-response is weaker than the text implies: significant at 1 year (HR 2.14, p=0.03) but absent at 2 years (p=0.66). That matters because the central tension of ultra-central SBRT is keeping ablative target dose while capping airway hotspots. The guideline resolves it by favoring 60 Gy/8 or 60 Gy/15 and accepting PTV undercoverage at the OAR interface, a trade that the LC data tolerate but do not prove harmless.

Three features should temper confidence in the toxicity estimate specifically. Most studies had median follow-up under two years, and fatal hemoptysis can arrive late. Publication bias was detected for every toxicity endpoint, and the direction of that bias is almost certainly toward under-reporting. Retrospective series also tend to attribute a late death to progression rather than to treatment. Each of these pushes the true fatal rate above 4%, not below.

What the paper changes is the framing of the decision. Ultra-central location is no longer a single risk category but a gradient set by distance from the trachea and main bronchi, endobronchial extension, and concomitant drugs, with the HILUS 4% versus 18% split by a 1 cm boundary as the clearest anchor. What it does not settle is the constraint for individual PBT substructures, whether 60 Gy/15 preserves control in endobronchial disease, and how long to hold systemic agents other than VEGF inhibitors. SUNSET and LUNGTECH are the prospective data that could confirm or overturn the constraint.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: Concomitant drugs drive fatal risk: VEGF inhibitor exposure within 30 days of SBRT carried fatal hemoptysis HR 16.9 (p<0.001), and antiplatelet/anticoagulant use appeared in 17 G5 hemoptysis cases. ISRS asks for a 3-4 wk VEGF-inhibitor gap, ≥2-3 days for targeted agents and ≥2 days for IO.

High Response Rates and Lasting Remissions After Low-Dose Involved Field Radiotherapy in Indolent Lymphomas
papers.abstract: Purpose: To study the response rates and duration of response after low-dose (4 Gy) involved field radiotherapy (LD-IF-RT) in patients with recurrent indolent lymphoma. Patients and Methods: A total of 109 assessable patients (304 symptomatic sites) were irradiated (53 males and 56 females; median age, 62 years; range, 35 to 93), including 98 patients with follicular lymphoma (43 grade 1 and 55 grade 2), nine extranodal marginal zone lymphomas of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue-type and two patients with lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma. Bulky disease (≥5 cm) was present in 52% of all patients. A median of two prior regimens (range, 0 to 11) preceded LD-IF-RT. The median time since diagnosis was 41 months (range, 2 to 358 months). Time to (local) progression was calculated according to the Kaplan-Meier method. Differences in response rates between treatments within the same patient were compared using the McNemar test. Results: The overall response rate was 92%; complete response was reached in 67 patients (61%), partial response in 34 patients (31%), stable disease in six patients (6%), and progressive disease in two patients (2%). The median time to progression was 14 months. The median time to local progression was 25 months. The 67 patients with complete response showed a median time to progression of 25 months and a median time to local progression of 42 months. None of the factors studied (age, sex, follicular lymphoma grade, radiotherapy regimen, number of previous regimens and previous history, number of positive sites or largest lymphoma diameter) were found to be related to response rate. Conclusion: LD-IF-RT is a valuable asset in the management of patients with follicular lymphoma and should be considered in patients with recurrent disease.
